summary:
Johor is one of Malaysia's thirteen states and stands under the national framework: federal law criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity across the country, and the state layer adds Sharia offences that reach Muslims alone. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code, in force in Johor, punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping. The provisions apply to men and women alike, cover acts that are consensual and private, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens.

Johor's Sharia enactment sits alongside that federal layer, prohibiting cross-dressing and "a man posing as a woman" together with liwat and musahaqah. State Sharia penalties under the national framework reach three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and the offences apply only to Muslims, so a non-Muslim visitor falls under the federal Penal Code alone. No enactment defines transgender dress in legal terms; whether presentation is compliant is decided by religious officers at the point of contact.

Johor's own record contains no protective or tolerant regime. In November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The national scale of such activity gives the announcement context: at least 1,733 people had attended "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown that has run since the 2018 general election.

Enforcement against consenting adults in private remains uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but prosecutorial discretion of that kind is not a legal protection and has been withdrawn under political pressure elsewhere in the country. Nothing in Johor narrows the penalties a visitor would face if charges were brought.

No rule of entry addresses gender identity or transition status. The nearest documented statement of national entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay. Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and same-sex marriage and partner recognition of any kind are unavailable.
tangentialFactors:
A Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters report of 10 August 2022 documented state-conducted investigations into LGBT people covering Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah. Johor is not named in that list, which reflects the scope of the investigation rather than an exemption for Johor.

Social venues have become a target of the national crackdown. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022; a magistrate rejected the request to extend remand on the ground that no case had been made out, yet more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Earlier operations include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and eleven shopping malls in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister said the provisions would be revisited, and police raided another sauna within days.

Violence against transgender women in Malaysia is lethal and largely unpunished. A trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing in fewer than two months, and reporting on those killings is obstructed by investigators' working assumptions. Arbitrary arrest is documented over decades, including a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014, repeated arrests of individual women more than twenty times, and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention.

Constitutional litigation has not removed the framework. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence rather than on the substance, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised. The High Court had earlier denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional.
localsOnly:
Residents of Johor who are Muslim fall under both the federal Penal Code and the state Sharia enactment, so cross-dressing charges, liwat and musahaqah are available to the state Islamic religious department in addition to the criminal offences that reach everyone. Sharia courts may also impose non-custodial institutional outcomes under the national framework: women convicted of musahaqah may be committed to an approved home for up to six months, and cross-dressing and other offenders may be ordered into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states, extended to a year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment.

The conversion-therapy centres announced by the Johor government in November 2023 are directed at people living in the state. The 1,733 recorded attendees of "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021 indicate that such programmes already operate through state machinery under the post-2018 crackdown.

Identity documents remain under state control. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holding that sex is determined at birth and unaffected by reassignment surgery, though never gazetted and not legally binding, is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card on the reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is a Johor case: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable to Johor residents, and no political party pursues LGBTQ legal reform; Mahathir told the Cambridge Union in June 2019 that Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage. July 2020 remarks by the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister, granting his department his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, prompted the International Commission of Jurists to demand the order be revoked.
outOfScopeNotes:
Johor's own Sharia enactment is not reproduced in this inventory, so the exact offence wording and penalty schedule applying in Johor specifically remains unresolved; the three-year, RM5,000 and six-stroke figures stated here are the national framework figures from the parent profile rather than a reading of the Johor statute.

Whether the Johor Islamic religious department has carried out cross-dressing or gender-nonconformity arrests in recent years is not sourced in this inventory. No record of such arrests appears here, and that absence should not be read as evidence that none occur.

The operational status of the conversion-therapy centres announced in November 2023 is unresolved: the announcement is documented, but whether centres opened, where, or how many people they have received is not sourced here.

Whether Johor's Sharia enactment provides for approved-home committal or compulsory counselling in the terms the parent framework describes for other states is not stated in this inventory; the Terengganu figures cited belong to a different state.
